title: Fit a power law in log space
goal:
Section 3 fits every trend as $L(X) = (X_c / X)^{\alpha_X}$ (Equations 3.1 to 3.3). Taking logs turns this into a line, $\ln L = \alpha \ln X_c - \alpha \ln X$, so an ordinary least-squares line fit recovers both constants.

Write three functions:

- `fit_power_law(x, y)` returns `(alpha, x_c)`.
- `predict(alpha, x_c, x)` evaluates $(x_c / x)^{\alpha}$.
- `extrapolate(x, y, x_new)` fits the line and returns `(y_pred, sd_log)`. `sd_log` is the one-sigma uncertainty of a new measurement at `x_new`, in log units, so the interval is $y_\text{pred}\, e^{\pm\,\text{sd\_log}}$. With $n$ points, residual variance $s^2 = \sum r_i^2 / (n - 2)$, and $S_{xx} = \sum (\ln x_i - \overline{\ln x})^2$, use

$$
\text{sd\_log}^2 = s^2\left(1 + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(\ln x_\text{new} - \overline{\ln x})^2}{S_{xx}}\right).
$$

The tests use synthetic losses drawn from the paper's Equation 1.1 constants.
hints: `np.polyfit(np.log(x), np.log(y), 1)` returns `(slope, intercept)`. The slope is $-\alpha$.
The intercept is $\alpha \ln x_c$, so $x_c = \exp(\text{intercept} / \alpha)$. Forgetting the division by $\alpha$ gives a scale that is off by many orders of magnitude.
Compute the residuals in log space: `ly - (slope * lx + intercept)`. Divide their sum of squares by `n - 2`, because the line used two fitted numbers.
The `1 +` inside the square root is the scatter of one new measurement. Without it you get the uncertainty of the fitted line only.
